source: Tardigrades, also called water bears, are microscopic animals about half a millimeter long that can survive conditions that would kill almost any other creature. When their surroundings dry out, they curl into a dormant shape called a tun, losing about 97 percent of their body water and slowing their metabolism to nearly nothing. In this state they have survived temperatures close to absolute zero, brief heating above 100 degrees Celsius, and intense radiation. In 2007, a European Space Agency experiment exposed dried tardigrades to open space for ten days, and some revived after being rehydrated. Researchers studying the species Ramazzottius varieornatus found a protein named Dsup that clings to DNA and shields it from radiation damage, which may explain part of their resilience.
target_summary: Tardigrades survive heat, cold, radiation and space by dehydrating into dormant tuns.

source: The Port Alder city council voted 9 to 4 on Tuesday to approve a bus rapid transit line that will run 14 kilometers from the harbor district to the Northgate university campus. The project is budgeted at PHP 2.4 billion, with 60 percent coming from a national infrastructure loan and the rest from city bonds. Planners expect 22 stations, dedicated center lanes, and buses arriving every four minutes during rush hour. Construction is scheduled to begin in March 2027 and to finish by late 2029, with a flat fare of PHP 15. Council members who opposed the plan said the loss of two traffic lanes on Mabini Avenue would worsen congestion and hurt street vendors, while supporters pointed to a city study projecting 80,000 daily riders within two years of opening.
target_summary: Port Alder approved a 14-kilometer, PHP 2.4 billion bus rapid transit line.

source: The Sunrise Bakers Cooperative reported third-quarter revenue of PHP 8.7 million, up 12 percent from the same period last year, driven mainly by a new line of pandesal bundles sold to neighborhood sari-sari stores. Flour prices rose 9 percent during the quarter, which cut the gross margin from 31 percent to 27 percent. To offset the higher costs, the cooperative signed a six-month bulk purchase agreement with a regional miller and replaced two aging ovens with gas-efficient models, cutting fuel spending by an estimated PHP 140,000 per quarter. Manager Lorna Reyes told members that the cooperative will pay a patronage refund of PHP 1,200 to each of its 85 member-bakers in December, but will postpone plans to open a second retail branch until at least the middle of next year.
target_summary: Sunrise Bakers' revenue rose 12 percent, but flour prices cut margins.

source: Around 1440, the German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg began developing a printing system in Mainz that used movable metal type, an oil-based ink, and a modified wine press. Earlier printers in East Asia had used carved wooden blocks and, later, ceramic or metal characters, but Gutenberg's alloy of lead, tin, and antimony made durable, uniform letters that could be rearranged for every page, which suited alphabetic scripts well. His 42-line Bible, completed around 1455, is the first major book printed this way in Europe, and roughly 180 copies are thought to have been made. By 1500, printing shops operated in more than 200 European cities, and the sharp drop in the cost of books helped spread literacy, standardize languages, and circulate new ideas such as those of the Protestant Reformation.
target_summary: Gutenberg's movable metal type printing, begun about 1440, made books cheap.

source: Sleep is not just rest for the body; it is an active period during which the brain organizes what it learned during the day. In deep, slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus appears to replay recent experiences, helping move them into long-term storage in the cortex. Rapid eye movement sleep, which occurs more often in the second half of the night, is linked to emotional processing and to making creative connections between separate ideas. Experiments show that people who sleep after studying generally remember more than people who stay awake for the same length of time, and cutting sleep short on the night after learning weakens retention. Most health agencies recommend that adults get at least seven hours per night, since regularly sleeping less is associated with poorer attention, mood, and memory.
target_summary: Sleep consolidates memories, so adults need at least seven hours.

source: Lithium-ion batteries lose capacity over time because of slow chemical side reactions inside each cell. During the first charge, a thin layer called the solid electrolyte interphase forms on the graphite anode and protects it, but the layer keeps growing with each cycle and permanently traps some lithium ions, leaving fewer available to carry charge. High temperatures speed up this growth, while charging quickly at low temperatures can cause metallic lithium to plate onto the anode, which reduces capacity and can create safety risks. Keeping a battery between about 20 and 80 percent charge and avoiding heat reduces stress on the cell. Many phone batteries are designed to keep roughly 80 percent of their original capacity after 500 full charge cycles.
target_summary: Lithium-ion batteries degrade as a growing anode layer traps lithium.

source: A provincial education office has released results from a six-month pilot that served hot lunches to pupils in 36 public elementary schools. Each meal cost PHP 25 and was prepared by parent volunteers using vegetables from school gardens and rice supplied by a local farmers' group. The program reached about 9,000 pupils from kindergarten to grade 3. Average daily attendance rose from 88 percent to 94 percent, and teachers reported fewer students leaving class early because of hunger. A follow-up health check found that the share of underweight children fell from 21 percent to 17 percent. The office plans to expand the program to 120 schools next school year but warned that the budget depends on continued support from the provincial government, which has covered 70 percent of the costs so far.
target_summary: A PHP 25 school lunch pilot raised attendance and cut underweight rates.

source: Compound interest means that interest is calculated on both the original amount and the interest already earned, so growth speeds up over time. For example, if you deposit PHP 10,000 in an account that pays 6 percent per year and leave it untouched, you will have about PHP 10,600 after the first year. After ten years, the balance will be roughly PHP 17,908, while simple interest on the same deposit would give only PHP 16,000. A common shortcut called the rule of 72 estimates how long it takes money to double by dividing 72 by the annual interest rate, so at 6 percent the balance doubles in about 12 years. The same effect works against borrowers, which is why unpaid credit card balances can grow so quickly.
target_summary: Compound interest grows balances faster because earned interest also earns interest.

source: A coastal conservation group has completed the first phase of a mangrove restoration project along a river delta, planting 120,000 seedlings across 85 hectares of former fishponds. Volunteers from six fishing villages carried out most of the planting over eighteen months, working alongside biologists who selected native species suited to each tidal zone. A survey conducted one year later found that 68 percent of the seedlings had survived, a figure that organizers described as above average for restoration work. Mangrove forests protect shorelines by reducing wave energy during storms, provide nursery habitat for fish and crabs, and store large amounts of carbon in their soil. The group says the second phase will add 150 hectares, and that villages will earn small payments for monitoring and replanting the sites.
target_summary: A group planted 120,000 mangrove seedlings on 85 hectares; 68 percent survived.

source: The Riverton Herons beat the Eastgate Falcons 98 to 91 on Saturday night, ending a four-game losing streak in front of a sold-out crowd of 6,200. Guard Miguel Santos led all scorers with 31 points and added eight assists, including a three-pointer with 1:12 left that put Riverton ahead by seven. Eastgate had led by six at halftime behind 58 percent shooting, but the Herons tightened their defense in the third quarter, forcing seven turnovers and outscoring the Falcons 29 to 15. Falcons center David Okafor finished with 22 points and 14 rebounds but fouled out with three minutes remaining. Riverton improves to 9 wins and 11 losses and will travel to face the Lakeshore Mariners on Wednesday.
target_summary: Riverton beat Eastgate 98-91, led by Santos's 31 points.

source: A new exhibition at the Harbor Street Museum, titled Threads of the Highlands, brings together more than 140 woven textiles from five mountain communities, dating from the late 1800s to the present. Curators arranged the pieces by pattern rather than by date, so visitors can see how zigzag and diamond designs, once used to signal clan identity, have been reinterpreted by younger weavers using synthetic dyes and recycled fabric. Several backstrap looms are on display, and on weekends, weavers from the participating communities demonstrate how a single blanket can take up to three months to finish. Admission is PHP 150 for adults and free for students, and the show runs through the end of January. Museum director Elena Cruz said the goal is to treat weaving as a living craft rather than a historical relic.
target_summary: A museum exhibition shows 140 highland textiles, treating weaving as living craft.

source: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun, yet Venus is hotter. Venus has a surface temperature of about 465 degrees Celsius, high enough to melt lead, and it stays almost the same on the day and night sides. The reason is its atmosphere, which is about 96 percent carbon dioxide and so thick that the pressure at the surface is roughly 90 times that of Earth. This creates a runaway greenhouse effect that traps heat from the Sun. Mercury, by contrast, has almost no atmosphere, so heat escapes quickly. Its daytime temperature can reach about 430 degrees Celsius, but at night the surface drops to around minus 180 degrees.
target_summary: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick atmosphere traps heat.

source: The Aerolite 14 is a lightweight laptop aimed at students and remote workers who want long battery life without paying for a premium brand. It weighs 1.2 kilograms, has a 14-inch screen with a 120 hertz refresh rate, and costs PHP 42,990 in the base configuration with 16 gigabytes of memory and a 512 gigabyte drive. In our tests, the battery lasted 13 hours of video playback, and the keyboard was comfortable for long typing sessions. The main weaknesses are a dim screen that is hard to read outdoors, a webcam that struggles in low light, and speakers that sound thin. Performance is fine for browsing, documents, and light photo editing, but the cooling fan becomes noticeably loud when the processor is under heavy load, so gamers and video editors should look elsewhere.
target_summary: The PHP 42,990 Aerolite 14 has strong battery life but weak screen.

source: Herd immunity happens when enough people in a community are immune to a disease that it can no longer spread easily, which indirectly protects infants and people who cannot be vaccinated. The share of the population that must be immune depends on how contagious the disease is, measured by the basic reproduction number, or R0, the average number of people one case would infect in a fully susceptible group. A simple formula gives the threshold as 1 minus 1 divided by R0. Measles has an R0 between 12 and 18, so roughly 92 to 94 percent of people need immunity, while a disease with an R0 of 2 needs only 50 percent. Because immunity is rarely spread evenly, outbreaks can still occur in pockets with low vaccination even when national averages look high.
target_summary: Herd immunity needs a share of immunity set by the disease's R0.

source: Rice farmers have traditionally kept their fields flooded, but a method called alternate wetting and drying lets them use less water without cutting yields. Instead of keeping fields under water all season, farmers allow the water to fall to about 15 centimeters below the soil surface, checked with a perforated tube pushed into the ground, and then reflood the field. Studies promoted by the International Rice Research Institute report water savings of 15 to 30 percent. The practice also lowers methane emissions, since flooded soils are a major source of this gas. Farmers must keep fields flooded during flowering, when rice is most sensitive to dry conditions, and they need reliable irrigation timing for the method to work. Some irrigation groups that adopted it also report lower pumping costs.
target_summary: Alternate wetting and drying saves rice farmers water without cutting yields.

source: The Panama Canal does not cut through the isthmus at sea level; instead, ships are lifted up and over it using a series of locks. Vessels entering from either ocean are raised in steps by about 26 meters to the level of Gatun Lake, cross the lake, and then are lowered on the other side. Each transit uses fresh water from the lake, which flows downhill by gravity, so there are no pumps. The canal opened in 1914, and a third set of larger locks was added in 2016 to allow bigger container ships. These new locks have water-saving basins that reuse roughly 60 percent of the water in each lockage. Because the system depends on rainfall, a severe drought in 2023 forced authorities to limit the number of daily crossings.
target_summary: The Panama Canal lifts ships over the isthmus using gravity-fed locks.

source: A transformer fire at the Kalinaw substation early Sunday morning cut power to about 41,000 households in three municipalities, according to the regional electric cooperative. Firefighters brought the blaze under control within 90 minutes, and no injuries were reported. Technicians restored electricity to roughly 25,000 customers by noon by rerouting power through neighboring lines, but about 16,000 households, mostly in the hillside barangays, were still without service by evening. Cooperative engineers said a replacement transformer must be trucked in from a warehouse four hours away and that they expect to install it by Tuesday. Water districts reported low pressure after pumping stations lost power, and the municipal governments opened two gymnasiums as temporary shelters. The cause of the fire is under investigation.
target_summary: A substation fire cut power to 41,000 households.

source: A study of 1,200 senior high school students in three cities compared how different study habits related to exam results. Students who spread their review across at least four sessions over two weeks scored an average of 11 points higher on a 100-point test than students who crammed the same total hours the night before. Those who practiced by answering questions from memory also outperformed students who only reread their notes, even though the rereaders felt more confident about the material. The researchers noted that the survey could not prove cause and effect, since students who plan ahead may also be more motivated in other ways. They recommend that schools teach spaced practice and self-testing directly, because few students in the sample reported using either method on their own.
target_summary: Spaced practice and self-testing beat cramming and rereading, a study found.

source: Adobo is often called the unofficial national dish of the Philippines, but its basic technique predates the Spanish arrival. Before refrigeration, Filipinos preserved meat and fish by cooking them in vinegar and salt, which slows spoilage. When Spanish colonizers encountered the dish in the 1500s, they named it adobo after their own word for marinade, even though the Philippine version is not the same as Spanish adobo. Today there are countless regional variations: some cooks add soy sauce, others use coconut milk, and some leave out soy sauce entirely to make a version called adobong puti. Most versions share garlic, black peppercorns, and bay leaves, and many people say adobo tastes better the next day, after the flavors have had time to settle into the meat.
target_summary: Adobo, meat cooked in vinegar and salt, predates Spanish rule.

source: When wildfire smoke drifts into cities, fine particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers, known as PM2.5, can pass deep into the lungs and bloodstream, and they are linked to asthma attacks, heart problems, and early death. Staying indoors helps, but smoke seeps in through gaps, and indoor levels can reach 70 percent of outdoor levels within a few hours. A study of 60 homes in the Calder region found that a portable air cleaner with a HEPA filter, which traps 99.97 percent of particles above 0.3 micrometers, reduced indoor PM2.5 by an average of 78 percent when it was run in a bedroom with the door closed. Health agencies advise choosing a unit rated for the size of the room, replacing filters every six to twelve months, and avoiding devices that produce ozone. People can also make low-cost filters by taping a furnace filter to a box fan, which also removes many particles.
target_summary: HEPA air cleaners reduced indoor wildfire smoke particles in a Calder study.

source: A solar-powered cold storage unit installed in the fishing village of Pesca Nueva has helped 140 local fishers keep their catch fresh and sell it at better prices. Before the unit opened in 2022, fishers had to sell fish within hours of landing, often to traders who paid 40 percent below city prices, since they knew the fish would spoil. The 20-tonne unit, which keeps fish at 2 degrees Celsius using panels on its roof and a bank of batteries, is run by a cooperative that charges 0.15 dollars per kilogram per day. Fishers now store fish for up to three days and sell to restaurants in the nearby city, and average incomes have risen by 35 percent. Post-harvest losses dropped from 25 percent to 6 percent. The 190,000 dollar project was funded by a development bank, and the cooperative hopes to open a second unit.
target_summary: Solar cold storage raised Pesca Nueva fishers' incomes 35 percent.

source: Surgical trainees at the Marlowe Teaching Hospital now practice complex operations on virtual reality simulators before touching a patient. The headsets and handheld controllers reproduce the look and feel of procedures such as removing a gallbladder, and the software records every movement, scoring speed, accuracy, and the amount of tissue damaged. In a trial of 80 trainees, those who completed ten hours of simulation made 38 percent fewer errors during their first real operations and finished them 20 percent faster than those who trained conventionally. Each simulator costs about 60,000 dollars, but the hospital estimates that the training saves money by reducing complications and the use of operating room time for teaching. Senior surgeons stress that simulation supplements rather than replaces experience, since it cannot capture the unpredictability of bleeding or unusual anatomy in a live patient.
target_summary: VR simulation training cut trainee surgeons' errors by 38 percent.

source: Since the country introduced a deposit return scheme for drink containers two years ago, the return rate for plastic bottles and cans has climbed from 54 percent to 87 percent. Shoppers pay an extra 15 cents on every bottle or can and receive it back when they return the empty container to a machine at a supermarket or collection point. The system has collected 3.1 billion containers, and the material is cleaner than that from curbside bins, so it can be turned into new food-grade bottles. Litter surveys show that containers on roadsides and beaches have fallen by 41 percent. Retailers, however, complain about the space and cost of handling returns, and about 9 percent of unclaimed deposits, worth 46 million dollars, remain with the scheme operator, which has promised to spend them on more collection machines.
target_summary: Deposit return scheme raised container return rates from 54 to 87 percent.

source: Salt was once so valuable that entire trade networks were built around it. In the Middle Ages, merchants in the mountain town of Haldern carried salt from mines on the northern plains along a 300-kilometer route, known as the Salt Road, to markets in the south, where it fetched five times the price. Before refrigeration, salt was the main way to preserve meat and fish, which made it essential for feeding armies, sailors, and cities through the winter. The ruler who controlled the mines collected a tax on every cartload, and in 1411 the tolls produced about a third of the town's revenue. The road lost importance after canal barges and, later, railways could move heavy cargo more cheaply in the nineteenth century. Today, hikers follow the old route, and inns along the way still display weights once used to measure salt.
target_summary: Haldern's Salt Road carried valuable salt to southern markets.

source: Ice floats on water because it is less dense than liquid water, which is unusual, since most substances become denser when they freeze. Water molecules are made of one oxygen and two hydrogen atoms, and they attract each other through hydrogen bonds. In liquid water, these bonds constantly break and re-form, letting the molecules sit close together. When water cools below 4 degrees Celsius and freezes at zero, the molecules lock into a rigid hexagonal pattern with a lot of empty space, making ice about 9 percent less dense than water. This property has important effects: a lake freezes from the top down, and the layer of ice insulates the water below, allowing fish and other organisms to survive the winter. If ice sank, lakes and oceans would freeze from the bottom up, and aquatic life would be far more difficult.
target_summary: Ice floats because hydrogen bonds make it about 9 percent less dense.

source: A community land trust in the city of Verdale has kept 220 homes affordable for more than a decade by separating the ownership of land from the ownership of houses. The nonprofit trust buys the land and keeps it permanently, while families buy only the house, at prices about 40 percent lower than the market, and lease the land for a fee of 40 dollars per month. When owners sell, they keep a share of any increase in value, typically 25 percent, but the resale price is capped so that the next family can also afford the home. Foreclosure rates among trust homeowners have been about one tenth of the local average. Critics say that capped resale limits wealth building, and the waiting list has 1,300 households. The trust is now working with the city to acquire vacant lots for 150 additional homes.
target_summary: Verdale's land trust keeps 220 homes affordable by owning the land.

When owners sell, they keep a share of any increase in value, typically 25 percent, but the resale price is capped so that the next family can also afford the home. Foreclosure rates among trust homeowners have been about one tenth of the local average. Critics say that capped resale limits wealth building, and the waiting list has 1,300 households. The trust is now working with the city to acquire vacant lots for 150 additional homes.
target_summary: Verdale's community land trust keeps 220 homes about 40 percent cheaper by owning the land and capping resale prices, with foreclosures a tenth of average; critics cite limited wealth building, and the trust plans 150 more homes.

source: Hearing loss in young children often goes unnoticed, yet it can delay speech and affect learning. A screening program in the Grantham school district tested the hearing of 9,200 children aged 4 to 7 using a quick five-minute test performed by trained volunteers. The test flagged 540 children, about 6 percent, for follow-up, and audiologists confirmed hearing loss in 310 of them, most often caused by fluid in the middle ear, which is usually treatable. Parents of 87 percent of the confirmed cases had not been aware of a problem. After treatment, teachers reported improved attention in class, and reading scores of treated children rose by an average of 11 percent over the following year. The program costs about 4 dollars per child, and the district is considering extending it to all primary schools and repeating it every two years.
target_summary: School hearing screening found hearing loss in 310 children.

source: Coffee leaf rust, a fungal disease, has destroyed millions of coffee plants across Central America since 2012, causing an estimated 3 billion dollars in losses and leaving thousands of farmers in debt. The fungus covers the leaves with orange powder, weakens the plants, and can halve harvests. In the highlands of Sorrel Valley, farmers have replaced susceptible trees with a new variety that resists the disease, developed by crossing arabica with a naturally resistant relative. The variety yielded 28 percent more than the old one and needed 60 percent less fungicide, though it takes three years before a new tree produces a harvest, and replanting costs about 5,000 dollars per hectare. Coffee roasters have started to pay a premium of 20 percent for beans from resistant trees. Experts say taste tests rate the new variety as comparable to traditional ones.
target_summary: Resistant coffee varieties help farmers fight leaf rust.

source: A pilot project in 150 homes of people over 75 who live alone has tested whether smart speakers can reduce loneliness and help with daily tasks. The devices were set up to read the news, remind people to take medicines, play music, and make video calls to relatives with a spoken command. After six months, 68 percent of participants used the speaker daily, and the share who reported feeling lonely fell from 46 to 33 percent. Medication reminders helped: missed doses fell by about a quarter. Some older people found the technology confusing, and a few were concerned that the device listens constantly, so the project provided a trained volunteer to visit and explain privacy settings. Researchers note that devices cannot replace human contact, and that the loneliness reduction was greatest for people who also received regular visits.
target_summary: Smart speakers reduced loneliness among seniors living alone.

source: Five years after the Coral Shelf Marine Reserve banned fishing in 22 percent of its waters, surveys show that the number of large fish inside the protected zone has tripled and that fish are on average 40 percent larger. Bigger fish produce many more eggs, and the larvae drift out of the reserve, boosting catches in surrounding waters by 15 percent. Fishermen initially opposed the ban because it closed good fishing grounds, and some lost income in the first two years, but a study of 120 boats found that the average catch per trip is now higher than before. Scientists also recorded a recovery of seagrass and coral cover, which provide shelter for young fish. The reserve is guarded by patrols and drones, and the government plans to extend protection to 30 percent of its waters by 2030.
target_summary: A fishing ban tripled large fish and boosted nearby catches.

source: Mobile money services have cut the cost of sending money home for migrant workers, which is important for the many families that depend on remittances. The average fee for sending 200 dollars through traditional banks and money transfer companies is about 6.2 percent, while sending it through mobile apps costs 3.1 percent on average. In the village of Maguay, where one in three households receives money from relatives abroad, the share of transfers arriving by phone rose from 12 percent in 2018 to 61 percent last year. Families said that they receive the money faster, within minutes instead of days, and that they no longer need to travel two hours to a town to collect cash. Savings from lower fees amount to about 18 dollars per household each year. Still, sending requires smartphones and identification, which excludes some workers.
target_summary: Mobile money halves remittance fees to about 3.1 percent.

source: Every January, the coastal town of Sandrova hosts a ten-day kite festival that attracts 60,000 visitors and kite makers from 22 countries. Teams fly giant kites up to 30 meters long, shaped like fish, dragons, and octopuses, which are launched on the beach when winds rise in the afternoon. Local families have made kites for generations, using split bamboo and paper, and a workshop tent teaches children to build their own for 3 dollars. The festival began in 1987 as a competition among fishermen, and it now brings in an estimated 5.5 million dollars for hotels and restaurants. Organizers have introduced rules to protect the beach, including a ban on single-use plastic and a limit on vehicles. Judges give prizes for height, design, and the best stunt, and the grand prize this year went to a 25-meter blue whale from a team in Vietnam.
target_summary: Sandrova's January kite festival draws 60,000 visitors.

source: Wheelchair basketball, one of the first Paralympic sports, is played on a standard court with a basket at the usual height, and players must dribble or pass the ball after every two pushes of their chair. The National Wheelchair Basketball League has grown from 6 teams to 18 since 2015, and last season's championship drew a crowd of 7,400. Players use light chairs with angled wheels for stability and quick turns, and each team's players are given points according to their level of physical function, with a total limit of 14.5 on the court so that teams are balanced. The Rollers, a club in the city of Tressel, runs a program for 90 young players, who attend practice twice a week, and its coach says that many participants gain confidence and friendships. The league's biggest challenge is funding, as each sports chair costs between 3,000 and 5,000 dollars.
target_summary: Wheelchair basketball league grew to 18 teams but needs funding.

source: Sustainable aviation fuel, made from used cooking oil, agricultural waste, or other non-fossil sources, can cut the lifecycle carbon emissions of a flight by up to 80 percent compared with ordinary jet fuel, and it can be mixed with it in existing engines. Production remains tiny, however: it accounted for less than 1 percent of the 100 billion gallons of jet fuel used last year, and it costs two to three times as much. A new plant in the town of Harlan, due to open in 2026, will convert 40 million gallons of waste fats and oils into fuel per year, enough to supply roughly 5 percent of the nearby airport's demand. Airlines have signed contracts to buy most of the output, and the government offers a tax credit of up to 1.75 dollars per gallon. Critics worry that the demand for feedstock may compete with food production.
target_summary: Sustainable aviation fuel cuts emissions up to 80 percent but remains scarce.

source: A laser produces a narrow beam of light in which all the waves have the same wavelength and move in step, which is why the light is so intense and spreads so little. The word stands for light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Inside a laser, energy is supplied to a material, such as a crystal or a gas, causing its atoms to jump to a higher energy state. When one excited atom releases its energy as a photon, the photon can trigger another atom to release an identical photon, and so on, in a chain reaction. Mirrors at each end of the material bounce the light back and forth, amplifying it, and one mirror is partially transparent to let a beam escape. Lasers are used for reading barcodes, cutting steel, performing eye surgery, and sending data through optical fibers.
target_summary: Lasers amplify light through stimulated emission to make narrow, intense beams.

source: At the Birchwood Primary School, children aged five to eight spend one morning each week in a nearby woodland, regardless of the weather, in a program known as forest school. They build shelters, identify plants, light small fires with adult supervision, and use hand tools such as saws. A two-year evaluation compared 120 participants with 120 classmates at similar schools and found that the forest school pupils scored higher on measures of confidence and cooperation and were absent less often. Teachers also noticed improved concentration after the outdoor sessions, though reading and math scores did not differ significantly. The program requires a trained leader and costs about 450 dollars per child per year, mostly for staff and waterproof clothing. Parents sometimes worry about injuries, but records show that there were 14 minor accidents, mostly scrapes and splinters, and no serious ones.
target_summary: Weekly forest school improved children's confidence and cooperation.

source: Confusion over date labels on food is thought to cause about 20 percent of household food waste. A best before date refers to quality, not safety: after that date, the food may lose flavor or texture but is generally still safe if it has been stored properly. A use by date, found on perishable foods such as fresh meat, fish, and ready-made salads, is about safety, and eating the food after that date can be risky because harmful bacteria may be present even if it looks and smells normal. Some products carry sell by dates, which are meant for stores to manage stock and are not for consumers. A survey of 3,000 shoppers found that 56 percent threw away food because of a best before date without checking its condition. Experts suggest that shoppers rely on their senses for foods with best before dates and freeze items before they expire.
target_summary: Best before dates concern quality, while use by dates concern safety.

source: Tree rings offer a record of past climate stretching back thousands of years. Each year, a tree adds a new ring of wood, and the width and density of the ring depend on growing conditions: wide rings usually mean a warm, wet year, while narrow rings suggest drought or cold. By matching patterns in living trees with those in old timbers, scientists have built continuous records, such as a chronology of more than 8,000 years from pine trees in northern Europe. A team from the Ashford Institute analyzed rings from 1,200 bristlecone pines in the mountains of the southwest and reconstructed rainfall for the past 3,000 years, finding that the region has experienced four droughts lasting more than 40 years. These findings suggest that the 20th century was relatively wet, and that planners may be underestimating the risk of long dry periods.
target_summary: Tree rings record past climate, revealing long droughts in the southwest.

source: A study that followed 9,500 nurses for 12 years found that those working rotating night shifts for more than ten years had a 19 percent higher risk of heart disease and a 25 percent higher risk of type 2 diabetes than those who worked only days. Researchers believe that shift work disrupts the body's internal clock, which regulates hormones, blood pressure, and metabolism, and also encourages poor sleep and irregular eating. The health risks appeared to fall when nurses moved back to day work, though it took about five years for the added heart risk to disappear. The authors recommend that employers schedule shifts so that workers have at least 11 hours between them, rotate shifts forward from mornings to evenings to nights, and limit the number of consecutive night shifts to three. Workers can help by keeping a consistent sleep schedule and using blackout curtains.
target_summary: Long-term night shift work raised nurses' heart disease and diabetes risk.

source: Stalactites and stalagmites form in limestone caves through the slow action of dripping water. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil, becoming a weak acid that dissolves limestone as it seeps through cracks in the rock. When the water reaches the cave ceiling, some of the dissolved carbon dioxide escapes into the cave air, and the calcium carbonate that the water carried is deposited as a tiny ring of calcite. Over thousands of years, successive rings build a hanging stalactite, and drops that fall to the floor create a stalagmite rising to meet it. These formations grow extremely slowly, usually about 0.13 millimeters a year, so a one-meter stalactite may be 7,500 years old. When they meet, they form a column. Touching them leaves oils that stop growth, so visitors are asked not to touch.
target_summary: Dripping water slowly builds stalactites and stalagmites from dissolved limestone.

source: A credit score is a number, usually between 300 and 850, that estimates how likely a person is to repay borrowed money. Lenders use it to decide whether to approve loans and what interest rate to charge. The score is calculated from information in a credit report, with five main factors: payment history, which accounts for about 35 percent, the amount of debt compared with available credit, about 30 percent, the length of credit history, about 15 percent, the mix of credit types, and recent applications for new credit. Paying bills on time and keeping credit card balances below 30 percent of the limit are the most effective ways to improve a score. A score above 740 typically qualifies for the best rates; on a 300,000 dollar mortgage, the difference between a good and a fair score can mean tens of thousands of dollars in extra interest over 30 years.
target_summary: Credit scores estimate repayment likelihood, mostly from payment history and debt use.

source: The Aurelia, an all-electric ferry that began operating between the islands of Brisk and Teller in January, is the largest battery-powered passenger vessel in the country, carrying 400 passengers and 60 cars on the 40-minute crossing. Its 4.3 megawatt-hour battery is recharged at both terminals in about 15 minutes during unloading, using fast chargers connected to the grid. The ferry costs about 38 million dollars, twice as much as a diesel one, but the operator estimates that it will save 2.6 million dollars per year in fuel and maintenance, and will pay for itself in 14 years. It cuts carbon dioxide emissions by 1,900 tonnes per year, while the quieter engines reduce noise for passengers and marine animals. The operator plans to convert two more vessels on its routes by 2029.
target_summary: The all-electric Aurelia ferry recharges in 15 minutes between crossings.

source: The city of Harwick has replaced 18,000 lead water pipes since 2019, about two thirds of the total, after tests found lead levels above the safety limit in 12 percent of homes sampled. Lead in drinking water can harm brain development in children and raise blood pressure in adults, and no level is considered completely safe. The 310 million dollar program pays to replace both the city's portion of each pipe and the homeowner's portion, which many residents could not otherwise afford, and crews have completed 120 replacements per week. Since the work began, the share of children with elevated blood lead levels has fallen from 5.1 to 2.9 percent. During construction, residents are advised to run taps for several minutes and use filters certified to remove lead. The city expects to finish the remaining 9,000 pipes by 2028.
target_summary: Harwick replaced 18,000 lead pipes and cut children's elevated lead levels.

source: Paleontologists working in the badlands of Montara have announced the discovery of a new species of plant-eating dinosaur, named Montarasaurus gracilis, that lived about 76 million years ago. The skeleton, found in 2021 by a student volunteer, is 85 percent complete, which is rare for such an old specimen, and shows an animal about 6 meters long with a duck-like bill and a row of bony plates along its back. Researchers say that the legs are unusually long and slender, suggesting that it could run fast to escape predators. A CT scan of the skull revealed large nasal passages that may have been used to produce loud calls. Preparing the fossil took 14 months of careful work with small tools and air-powered pens. The skeleton will go on display at the state museum next spring, and the research was published in the Journal of Paleontology.
target_summary: Paleontologists announced Montarasaurus gracilis, a new, long-legged duck-billed dinosaur.

source: Before mechanical refrigeration, people preserved food with salt, smoke, or ice cut from frozen lakes and rivers and stored in insulated icehouses. In the 1800s, the ice trade became big business: ships carried blocks of ice from New England to the Caribbean and India. The first practical refrigeration machine was built in 1834 by the inventor Jacob Perkins, who used ether in a closed cycle of compression and evaporation, and the principle remains the basis of modern refrigerators. In the 1860s, refrigerated railway cars began to carry meat and fruit over long distances, changing diets and allowing cities to grow. Household refrigerators appeared in the 1910s, but the early models were expensive and dangerous because they used toxic gases such as ammonia. By 1950, about 80 percent of homes in the country had a refrigerator.
target_summary: Refrigeration evolved from ice harvesting to Perkins's 1834 machine and household fridges.

source: The Inti Wasi weaving cooperative in the Peruvian Andes brings together 160 women who use traditional techniques to produce textiles from alpaca wool dyed with plants and minerals. Patterns woven into the cloth tell stories of the mountains, animals, and festivals, and each piece takes between two weeks and four months to complete. Before the cooperative was founded in 2008, weavers sold to middlemen who paid about 8 dollars for a shawl that was resold for 90 dollars in tourist markets. Now the cooperative sells directly to shops and online customers, and weavers receive 55 percent of the sale price, an average of 140 dollars per shawl. Income from weaving has paid for school fees and housing improvements. The group also runs workshops for girls to learn the craft, helping to preserve skills that were fading as young people moved to cities.
target_summary: Inti Wasi weavers earn more by selling directly instead of through middlemen.

source: A 17-kilometer cycle superhighway opened in the Greater Lowmoor region in May, connecting five towns to the city center with a wide, separated path that has no traffic lights or intersections with roads. Built for 61 million dollars, the path is 4 meters wide, lit at night, and includes bridges and tunnels that allow cyclists to avoid junctions. Counters show that an average of 7,800 people use it each day, more than twice the forecast, and a survey found that 28 percent of them previously traveled by car. The route is ideal for electric bicycles, which have helped many commuters who live as far as 15 kilometers from their jobs. Winter maintenance, including snow clearing, will cost about 400,000 dollars a year. Planners say there will be 90 kilometers of similar paths by 2032, and that each will be connected to train stations.
target_summary: Lowmoor's cycle superhighway carries 7,800 riders daily.

source: A network of low-orbit satellites has brought high-speed internet to the remote farming district of Eastholm, where cable and fiber were never built because the area has only 3 people per square kilometer. Customers install a dish about the size of a pizza box, which connects to satellites orbiting at 550 kilometers, much closer than traditional communications satellites, and this reduces delay to about 40 milliseconds. Tests by the regulator found average download speeds of 120 megabits per second, enough for video calls and online schooling. The service costs 99 dollars per month, plus 450 dollars for equipment, which many families find expensive, so the government offers a subsidy of 200 dollars. Farmers use the connection for equipment monitoring and sales. However, speeds fall during evening peak times, and astronomers worry that thousands of satellites interfere with observation.
target_summary: Low-orbit satellites brought 120-megabit internet to remote Eastholm.

source: Many products advertise themselves as whole grain, but the labels can be misleading. A whole grain contains all three parts of the kernel: the fiber-rich bran, the nutrient-rich germ, and the starchy endosperm, while refined grains retain only the endosperm. A review of 45 studies found that eating three servings of whole grains a day was linked to a 22 percent lower risk of heart disease. A bread described as multigrain, made with wheat flour, or stone ground is not necessarily whole grain, since these terms say nothing about whether the grains are intact. Nutritionists recommend checking that the first ingredient is a whole grain, such as whole wheat, oats, or brown rice, and that the product contains at least 3 grams of fiber per serving. Many whole grain breads contain added sugar, so the ingredients list should also be checked.
target_summary: Whole grain labels can mislead; check that whole grain is the first ingredient.

source: A wildlife corridor 4 kilometers long and 600 meters wide, completed in 2023, now links two forest reserves in southern Karnata that were cut off from each other by farms and a highway. Before the corridor, elephants traveling between the reserves often entered fields and destroyed crops, leading to 38 human deaths and 11 elephant deaths in five years. Conservationists bought land from 140 farmers, who were compensated at 1.4 times market value, and built an underpass beneath the highway that is 12 meters high. Camera traps recorded 310 elephant crossings in the first year, and incidents of crop damage in nearby villages fell by 62 percent. The project cost 14 million dollars. Villagers are also given early warnings by text message when elephants approach, and have received beehive fences, which elephants avoid.
target_summary: A 4-kilometer corridor linked two reserves, reducing elephant crop damage 62 percent.

source: Drowning is a leading cause of accidental death among children aged one to four, and most drownings happen within seconds, often when a child is unsupervised near water. A program in the Clearwater district has taught 5,400 children to swim since 2019 through subsidized lessons at 14 community pools, costing families 5 dollars per session. A study found that the number of child drownings in the district fell from seven in 2018 to two last year, and that children who completed the 12-lesson course were four times more likely to be able to swim 25 meters unaided. Instructors also teach water safety, such as how to float, how to wear a life jacket, and what to do if someone falls in. The program has a waiting list of 1,900 children, and pool operators say that a shortage of lifeguards limits capacity.
target_summary: Subsidized swim lessons cut child drownings in Clearwater from seven to two.

source: First-generation college students, who are the first in their families to attend university, are less likely to complete a degree than their peers: 54 percent graduate within six years compared with 69 percent of others. The University of Brannigan has tried to close the gap with a mentoring program that pairs each first-year student with a senior or alumnus who meets them every two weeks to help with study skills, finances, and navigating university systems. In the first three cohorts, 1,100 students took part, and 81 percent of them returned for their second year, compared with 70 percent of a matched group who did not participate. Mentors are volunteers who attend a six-hour training, and the program costs about 260 dollars per student. Students said that the most valuable aspect was having someone to ask basic questions without embarrassment.
target_summary: A mentoring program raised first-generation students' second-year return to 81 percent.

source: Tornado warnings now give people an average of 13 minutes to take shelter, up from 5 minutes in 1990, thanks to improvements in radar and forecasting. Doppler radar can detect the rotation inside a thunderstorm that often precedes a tornado, allowing forecasters to issue warnings before the funnel touches the ground. Research shows that each extra minute of lead time reduces the risk of death, and the best results occur with warnings of 8 to 20 minutes, since longer warnings can make people complacent. Still, around 70 percent of warnings turn out to be false alarms, and surveys show that many people are unsure what to do. Experts advise moving to the lowest floor of a sturdy building, away from windows, and not trying to outrun a tornado in a car. Weather agencies are testing phone alerts that show the warning area on a map.
target_summary: Tornado warning lead times rose from 5 to 13 minutes.

source: Each year, about 1.5 billion tires reach the end of their lives worldwide, and many end up in landfills or stockpiles, where they can catch fire and breed mosquitoes. One way to reuse them is to grind them into rubber crumbs and mix them into asphalt for roads. The city of Dunmore resurfaced 28 kilometers of roads with rubberized asphalt over three years, using the equivalent of 190,000 tires. Engineers say that the surface lasts about 30 percent longer, reduces tire noise by up to 5 decibels, and cuts maintenance costs. It costs about 15 percent more to lay than ordinary asphalt, but life-cycle savings offset the difference. Critics note concerns about chemicals leaching from the rubber into runoff, and the city is monitoring water samples near the roads. Several other cities have asked to review the results.
target_summary: Dunmore paved roads with tire-rubber asphalt that lasts longer.

source: A study of 1,300 families found that children whose parents read to them at least five times a week before age five had vocabularies about 1.4 million words larger by kindergarten than those who were never read to, an estimate based on the number of words children hear in books. Books contain more rare words than everyday conversation, which exposes children to new vocabulary and sentence structures. The benefit was larger when parents talked about the story, asking questions such as what a character might feel or what will happen next, instead of just reading the words. Children who were read to were also more likely to be interested in reading later. The study's authors recommend that families read for 15 minutes a day, and that libraries provide free books. They note that there are many ways to build language, including singing and storytelling, for parents who find reading difficult.
target_summary: Reading aloud before age five greatly expands children's vocabularies.

source: The small town of Garnet Falls has revived its Main Street through a low-interest loan program for businesses, started in 2019 with 2 million dollars from the state and local banks. Entrepreneurs can borrow up to 75,000 dollars at 2 percent interest to renovate a storefront or start a shop, and applicants must show a business plan and agree to remain open at least five days a week. In four years, 31 loans have been issued, 24 new businesses have opened, and the vacancy rate on Main Street has fallen from 34 percent to 9 percent. Repayment has been on track for all but two borrowers. The mix of shops now includes a bakery, a bookstore, a repair shop, and a brewery, and weekend foot traffic has doubled. The town now hopes to use the repaid funds to support another 40 businesses.
target_summary: Garnet Falls' loan program cut Main Street vacancies from 34 to 9 percent.

source: Before the 1880s, each town in the country kept its own local time, set by the position of the sun at noon, so that when it was noon in the capital it was a few minutes earlier or later in places a hundred kilometers away. This did not matter when travel was slow, but the spread of railways made it chaotic: timetables listed arrivals in dozens of different local times, causing confusion and accidents. On 18 November 1883, the railway companies introduced four standard time zones, and most towns adopted them within a year. A law that made standard time official came only in 1918. The change was not welcomed by everyone; some newspapers complained that the railways were dictating time itself, and some towns kept their old clocks for years. Today time zones are essential to scheduling and communication.
target_summary: Railways introduced standard time zones in 1883, replacing local solar times.

source: In autumn, leaves change from green to brilliant shades of yellow, orange, and red because of chemical changes triggered by shorter days and cooler temperatures. During summer, leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll, a pigment that absorbs sunlight to make sugars. As days shorten, trees stop producing chlorophyll and the existing supply breaks down, revealing yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids, which were present all along. Red and purple colors, however, come from anthocyanins, which are made in autumn from sugars trapped in the leaf. The most vivid displays occur after a warm, sunny fall with cool nights, since sunny days promote sugar production and cold nights, above freezing, prevent sugars from leaving the leaf. Drought or an early frost can dull the colors. Eventually, a layer of cells at the base of the stem seals off the leaf, which falls.
target_summary: Autumn leaves change color as chlorophyll breaks down and anthocyanins form.

source: The Westbrook Community Emergency Response Team, a group of 210 trained residents, has become a model for neighborhood preparedness. Volunteers complete a 20-hour course covering first aid, fire safety, search and rescue, and how to organize their neighbors after a disaster, and they practice twice a year with the fire department. When a flood struck in October, 60 team members went door to door to check on elderly residents, set up a shelter in the school gym that housed 140 people, and distributed supplies for three days before official help arrived. City officials say that volunteers like these can be vital, because emergency services are overwhelmed in the first hours of a major disaster. The team is financed with a 15,000 dollar annual grant and donations, and has started a program training teenagers.
target_summary: Westbrook's 210 trained volunteers aided residents during an October flood.

source: Cuneiform, one of the earliest writing systems, was invented in Mesopotamia around 3400 BCE, when scribes pressed a reed stylus into soft clay tablets to make wedge-shaped marks. At first, the marks recorded practical matters such as grain, livestock, and taxes, but over time the script was used for letters, laws, poems, and scientific texts. More than 500,000 tablets have been found, of which only a small fraction have been translated, partly because the script was used for 3,000 years and adapted to at least 15 languages. The Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest surviving stories, was recorded on twelve tablets in the seventh century BCE. Fired clay lasts far longer than paper, and tablets burned in destroyed cities were often baked hard, which preserved them. Researchers now use machine learning to help read damaged tablets.
target_summary: Cuneiform, invented in Mesopotamia around 3400 BCE, pressed wedges into clay tablets.

source: Certified timber carries a label showing that the wood comes from a forest managed to meet environmental and social standards, such as limits on clear-cutting, protection of wildlife habitat, and respect for the rights of local communities. Independent auditors visit forests every year, and they track wood from the forest to the store through a system of paper records. About 11 percent of the world's forests are certified, but most of them are in Europe and North America, while tropical forests, where deforestation is worst, make up only a small share. Studies show that certification can reduce illegal logging and improve worker safety, but results vary, and some groups argue that audits are too lenient. Buyers who want sustainable wood can look for the label on furniture and paper, and ask retailers for the origin of the timber.
target_summary: Certified timber shows wood came from forests meeting environmental and social standards.

source: A program that gave free eye exams and glasses to students in 40 schools in the Delmont district found that vision problems were much more common than parents expected. Of the 7,800 children screened, 1,420, about 18 percent, needed glasses, and nearly two thirds of them had never had an eye exam. Within a month, children received glasses made on site by a mobile optician, at a cost of 38 dollars per pair. A year later, reading scores of students who received glasses had risen by an average of 0.2 grade levels more than those of a comparison group, and teachers reported that they paid more attention in class. Poor vision is often mistaken for laziness or learning disabilities, so many children go for years without help. The district wants to include eye exams in the routine health checks required for school entry.
target_summary: Free school eye exams found 18 percent of children needed glasses.

source: The Lakeline bus rapid transit corridor, which opened in March, runs 14 kilometers across the city of Torrance Heights on dedicated lanes, giving buses a clear road away from traffic. Passengers board through wide doors at raised platforms, like a train, and pay before boarding, which cuts the time a bus spends at stops. Buses arrive every four minutes at peak hours, and the trip takes 28 minutes, compared with 51 minutes before. Ridership on the route has risen by 64 percent to 46,000 people per weekday, and the project cost 120 million dollars, about one tenth the cost of a light rail line of the same length. Some businesses along the road complained about the loss of parking spaces during construction, but a survey found that most shops now report more customers. source: After a major earthquake destroys buildings and roads, rescue teams often lack up-to-date maps of the affected area. Volunteers around the world now help by tracing buildings, roads, and bridges on satellite images and adding them to a free, open map database. After a quake in the Sorrel Highlands last year, 6,200 volunteers from 90 countries mapped 410,000 buildings in the first four days, a task that would have taken a professional team several months. Rescue organizations used the maps to plan routes, find damaged areas, and send supplies to villages that had not appeared on any official map. Accuracy is checked by experienced mappers, who reviewed about one in five contributions, and the error rate was below 3 percent. Organizers say that the maps also help later, when communities rebuild and plan evacuation routes for future disasters.
target_summary: Volunteers mapped 410,000 buildings in four days after a Sorrel quake.

source: Conventional cotton uses about 16 percent of the world's insecticides, and many of the chemicals harm farmers and wildlife. Organic cotton, grown without synthetic pesticides or fertilizers, accounts for less than 1 percent of production. In the Marwa region of India, 3,000 farmers switched to organic methods with support from a clothing company, planting cotton with beans and marigolds that attract beneficial insects and using compost instead of chemical fertilizer. Yields in the first two years were about 20 percent lower, but farmers spent 40 percent less on inputs and received a premium price of 25 percent, so profits were similar to those of conventional farms. Farmers also report fewer health problems. Organic cotton requires more land to produce the same amount of fiber, and the certification process is expensive, which keeps small farmers from joining.
target_summary: Organic cotton avoids synthetic pesticides, yielding less but cutting farmer input costs.

source: Seasons occur because the Earth's axis is tilted by 23.5 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit around the sun, and not because the planet is closer to the sun in summer. In fact, the Earth is closest to the sun in early January, when it is winter in the Northern Hemisphere. As the planet orbits, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the sun for half of the year, receiving more direct sunlight and longer days, which produces summer. Six months later, it is tilted away, so sunlight arrives at a lower angle and is spread over a larger area, and days are shorter, which produces winter. Near the equator the tilt has little effect, so those regions have wet and dry seasons instead of hot and cold ones. At the poles, the sun stays above the horizon for months in summer.
target_summary: Seasons result from Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt, not distance from the sun.

source: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, and it changes constantly because of supply and demand in currency markets. If the exchange rate between the dollar and the euro is 1.10, one euro buys 1.10 dollars. Several factors influence it, including interest rates, since higher rates attract foreign investors who need the currency to buy assets, inflation, which reduces a currency's purchasing power, and expectations about economic growth. A weaker currency makes a country's exports cheaper for foreign buyers and imports more expensive for its citizens. For travelers, a drop of 10 percent in the home currency means a 1,000 dollar holiday abroad costs about 1,100 dollars. Some governments fix their exchange rate to another currency, but doing so requires large reserves, and fixed rates can break down under pressure.
target_summary: Exchange rates, driven by supply and demand, make currencies weaker or stronger.

source: Overuse injuries, caused by repeated stress on muscles, tendons, and bones without enough time to heal, now make up about half of all sports injuries among children and teenagers. A review of 2,900 young athletes found that those who specialized in a single sport before age 12 and played it for more than eight months a year were 70 percent more likely to suffer an overuse injury than athletes who played several sports. Common problems include stress fractures, swimmer's shoulder, and pain in the growth plates of the heel and knee. Pediatricians advise that young athletes take at least one day off per week and two to three months a year away from any single sport, and that weekly training hours should not exceed a child's age in years. Coaches are encouraged to vary activities and to listen when children report pain.
target_summary: Single-sport specialization raised young athletes' overuse injury risk by 70 percent.

source: The Hollow Valley Folk Archive, a collection of 6,400 field recordings made between 1948 and 1985, has been digitized and released online for free. The recordings, made on reel-to-reel tape by the folklorist Ruth Calloway, include ballads, work songs, fiddle tunes, and spoken stories from 320 farming and mining communities, many sung by people who had no other chance to record their music. The project, which took four years and 410,000 dollars, involved cleaning the tapes, repairing broken reels, and transcribing lyrics, with help from 200 volunteers. Within a month of launch, the site had 120,000 listeners, and several contemporary bands have recorded their own versions of songs found in the archive. Descendants of the singers can submit corrections and memories, which are added to each recording's page, and about 900 families have already contributed.
target_summary: Hollow Valley's 6,400 folk recordings from 1948 to 1985 are now free online.

source: When oil spills into the sea, some microbes can help clean it up. Certain bacteria naturally feed on hydrocarbons, breaking oil down into carbon dioxide and water, and their populations multiply quickly near a spill. After a tanker leaked 12,000 tonnes of crude oil off the coast of Varnes in 2019, scientists sprayed a mixture of nutrients, mostly nitrogen and phosphorus, on 40 kilometers of oiled shoreline to speed the growth of these bacteria. On treated beaches, oil levels dropped by 70 percent in 90 days, compared with 35 percent on untreated beaches nearby. This approach, called bioremediation, is cheaper and less harmful than scrubbing rocks with hot water, but it works slowly and is less effective in cold waters. Responders still use booms and skimmers first to remove as much oil as possible.
target_summary: Nutrients sprayed on oiled beaches sped bacterial oil breakdown.

source: A survey of 3,400 graduates found that students who completed paid internships received on average 1.4 job offers before graduation, compared with 0.7 for those who did unpaid internships and 0.6 for those with no internship. Paid interns also reported starting salaries 11 percent higher, about 4,600 dollars a year. Researchers believe paid internships tend to involve real responsibilities and training, whereas unpaid ones are more often limited to routine tasks. Unpaid positions also favor students whose families can support them, as 62 percent of unpaid interns said that they depended on family money to cover living costs, compared with 31 percent of those paid. Employers surveyed said that the cost of paying interns, about 6,000 dollars per placement, is worth it for a chance to recruit. Several universities now offer stipends to students who take unpaid internships.
target_summary: Paid internships brought more job offers and higher salaries than unpaid ones.

source: Smallpox killed an estimated 300 million people in the twentieth century alone before it was eradicated, making it one of the deadliest diseases in history. In 1796, the English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who caught cowpox seemed protected against smallpox, and he tested the idea by inoculating a boy with material from a cowpox sore and later exposing him to smallpox, without the boy falling ill. The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow. Vaccination spread across the world, and in 1967 the World Health Organization began an intensified campaign using a strategy of finding outbreaks and vaccinating everyone around each case. The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 the WHO declared smallpox eradicated, the only human disease to have been eliminated so far.
target_summary: Jenner's 1796 cowpox experiment led to smallpox vaccination and eradication in 1980.

source: Online shoppers rely heavily on reviews: a survey found that 93 percent of consumers read them before making a purchase. However, an estimated 10 to 15 percent of reviews on major platforms are fake, written by paid reviewers or generated by software to boost ratings. A team of researchers at the Corvin Institute built a program that flags suspicious reviews by analyzing patterns such as sudden bursts of five-star ratings, repeated phrases across different products, and reviewers who post many reviews in a single day. The tool correctly identified 88 percent of known fake reviews, while wrongly flagging 4 percent of genuine ones. Consumers can protect themselves by looking at the middle ratings, checking whether reviewers are verified buyers, and being wary of reviews that are vague or unusually enthusiastic. Regulators in several countries have begun to fine companies that buy fake reviews.
target_summary: Up to 15 percent of online reviews are fake; a tool detects most.

source: A passive house is a building designed to use up to 90 percent less energy for heating and cooling than a conventional one, through very thick insulation, airtight construction, triple-glazed windows, and a ventilation system that recovers heat from outgoing air. A primary school built to this standard in the town of Kellerby uses about 15 kilowatt-hours of heating energy per square meter per year, compared with 140 for the older school it replaced. The building cost 6 percent more than a standard school, but energy bills are 82 percent lower, and the extra investment will be recovered in nine years. Teachers said that classrooms stay comfortable and quiet, and that the fresh air system keeps carbon dioxide levels low, which can improve concentration. Builders say that passive house techniques are not hard, but require careful workmanship, since small gaps in insulation can cause large losses.
target_summary: A passive house school cut heating energy about 90 percent.

source: Beans, lentils, chickpeas, and other legumes are rich in protein and fiber, and they are among the cheapest and most climate-friendly foods. A cup of cooked lentils contains about 18 grams of protein and 16 grams of fiber, and costs less than 50 cents. A large study that followed 40,000 adults for 12 years found that those who ate legumes four or more times a week had a 22 percent lower risk of heart disease than those who ate them less than once a week. Growing legumes also produces far fewer greenhouse gases than raising meat, and the plants add nitrogen to the soil, reducing the need for fertilizer. Nutritionists note that legumes can cause gas, which can be reduced by soaking and rinsing dried beans, cooking them thoroughly, and increasing intake gradually. Despite the benefits, the average person eats legumes only about twice a week.
target_summary: Legumes are cheap, protein-rich, climate-friendly foods linked to lower heart disease risk.

source: Girls make up only 28 percent of students in advanced physics and computer science courses at schools in the Harlan region, even though they perform as well as boys in math. An after-school program called Code Sisters, which began in 2020 with five schools, now operates in 41 schools and has 1,900 members. Girls aged 11 to 16 meet weekly to build apps, program robots, and meet women who work as engineers and scientists. A follow-up survey found that 61 percent of participants said they were considering a career in technology, compared with 22 percent of girls who were not in the program. Girls who attended for at least two years were twice as likely to choose a computer science course in high school. The program is free, funded by local companies, and led by volunteer mentors, and its organizers say that the biggest need is for more women willing to volunteer.
target_summary: Code Sisters grew to 41 schools, boosting girls' technology career interest.

source: The Global Positioning System works by measuring the time it takes for signals to travel from satellites to a receiver. About 31 satellites orbit the Earth at an altitude of roughly 20,200 kilometers, and each one continuously broadcasts its position and the exact time from an atomic clock on board. A receiver, such as a phone, picks up signals from at least four satellites and calculates how far away each one is by multiplying the signal's travel time by the speed of light. With distances from four satellites, the receiver can determine its position in three dimensions, as well as correct its own clock. The accuracy of a smartphone is typically within five meters outdoors. Because satellites move fast and are high above Earth's gravity, their clocks run at a slightly different rate, and the system must correct for this relativistic effect.
target_summary: GPS calculates position from signal travel times from at least four satellites.

source: A food forest in the Eastmoor neighborhood turns half a hectare of former wasteland into a garden that imitates the layers of a natural forest, with tall nut and fruit trees, shrubs such as currants and hazelnuts, herbs, root crops, and climbing plants. Volunteers planted 420 trees and shrubs in 2019, and by last year the forest produced about 2.3 tonnes of fruit and vegetables, all free for residents to harvest. Because the plants are mostly perennial and support each other, the forest needs little watering and almost no fertilizer, and it supports bees, birds, and other wildlife. Organizers say that after the first three years of establishment, maintenance takes about four hours a week. Some neighbors initially worried about pests and mess, but the group holds monthly harvest days and workshops, and about 150 people take part. The city is considering a second site.
target_summary: Eastmoor's food forest yields 2.3 tonnes of free produce from layered plantings.
